content: The mention of any company or product name does not imply endorsement by the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH). Copies of this and other NIOSH documents are available. Definitions are quoted, where possible, from the relevant American National Standards Institute (ANSI) standards, such as ANSI S1.1-1994 or ANSI S3.20-1995, under the terms used in those standards. The fence is the hearing threshold level above which a material impairment of hearing is considered to have occurred. Frequency is defined as the reciprocal of the period for a function periodic in time. The unit of frequency is hertz (Hz), as per ANSI S1.1-1994. The hearing threshold level (HTL) for a specified signal is the amount in decibels by which the hearing threshold for a listener, for one or both ears, exceeds a specified reference equivalent threshold level. The unit is decibels (dB), as defined in ANSI S1.1-1994.g., months, years). Impact refers to a single collision of one mass in motion with another mass, which may be in motion or at rest, as defined in ANSI S1.1-1994. Impulse is the product of a force and the time during which the force is applied. More specifically, impulse is the time integral of force from an initial time to a final time. Impulsive noise is characterized by a sharp rise and rapid decay in sound levels, lasting less than one second. For the purposes of this document, it refers to impact or impulse noise. Intermittent noise refers to noise levels that are interrupted by intervals of relatively low sound levels. Noise is defined as (1) undesired sound or (2) erratic, intermittent, or statistically random oscillations. By extension, noise can also refer to any unwarranted disturbance within a useful frequency band, such as undesired electric waves in a transmission channel or device. The noise reduction rating (NRR) indicates a hearing protector's noise reduction capabilities. It is a single-number rating required by law to be displayed on the label of each hearing protector sold in the United States. The unit is decibels (dB). Permanent threshold shift (PTS) refers to a permanent increase in the threshold of audibility for an ear. The unit is decibels (dB), as defined in ANSI S3.20-1995. The pulse range is the difference in decibels between the peak level of an impulsive signal and the root-mean-square level of a continuous noise. A significant threshold shift is a shift in hearing threshold, outside the range of audiometric testing variability (±5 dB), that warrants follow-up action to prevent further hearing loss. NIOSH defines a significant threshold shift as an increase in the HTL of 15 dB or more at any frequency (500, 1000, 2000, 3000, 4000, or 6000 Hz) in either ear, confirmed for the same ear and frequency by a second test within 30 days of the first test., in a medium with internal forces (elastic or viscous), or the superposition of such propagated oscillations, or (2) the auditory sensation evoked by the oscillation described above. Sound intensity is the average rate of sound energy transmitted in a specified direction at a point through a unit area normal to this direction at the point considered. The unit is watts per square meter (W/m²), symbolized as I. Sound intensity level is ten times the logarithm to the base ten of the ratio of the intensity of a given sound in a stated direction to the reference sound intensity of 1 picowatt per square meter (pW/m²). The unit is decibels (dB), symbolized as L. The unit is pascal (Pa), as defined in ANSI S1.1-1994. The unit is decibels (dB), symbolized as Lp. Such a shift may also be caused by other means, such as the use of aspirin or other drugs. The unit is decibels (dB), as defined in ANSI S3.20-1995. TWA = 10 × Log(D/100) + 85, where D = dose. Varying noise refers to noise, with or without audible tones, for which the level varies substantially during the period of observation.
